speechtext: Mr. GEOFFRION moved that the third report of the special committee appointed to investigate the Lumsden charges be concurred in.

This report asks that leave be granted the committee to employ counsel for the purpose^ of assisting' them in the investigation of matters referred to them. The question of employing counsel is a very important one, and I propose to offer a few remarks regarding the advisability of adopting this report. We have had in discussion in the committee the question of counsel. Yesterday, Mr. Smith, of Montreal, appeared before the committee as counsel for the commission. The matter to be investigated arises out of statements made by Mr. Lums-den in his letter of resignation. Mr. Lumsden in that letter said that the classifications on the road had not been in accordance with his instructions, and that in effect they were so erroneous that it was quite clear his instructions had been entirely ignored by a certain section of the engineering staff. That statement necessarily reflects upon the manner in which the road is being constructed. The commission appointed by the government is responsible to see that not only competent but thoroughly _ honest engineers are employed; and prima facie if the engineers have not satisfactorily carried out the work, the commission is to blame. The commission would be in a very deplorable position if it should turn out that, with its connivance, the engineering staff had deliberately conspired to defraud the public, but it would still be in an unfortunate position if the fault was due simply to incompetency or carelessness on the part of the staff. The charge, therefore, of Mr. Lumsden, is necessarily a charge against the commission, and it is important to it that it should clear its skirts by showing that there has been nothing wrong at all. On the other hand, it is in the public interest that this matter should be thoroughly probed; and if any wrong-doing has taken place, that it should be exposed and put a stop to, and that those responsible should be made known. The commission has appointed as counsel, Mr. Smith, to represent it. The commission is appointed by the government and is responsible for its engineers just as the government is responsible for the commission.
So the government are responsible for the acts of these engineers who are now charged with wrong-doing in the letter of resignation of Mr. Lumsden. Therefore we have this effect that we have counsel representing the one side and the one side only. It has been suggested that as Mr. Lumsden does not desire counsel, that is therefore an end of the matter. After discussion upon that matter the committee has come to the conclusion that it will be necessary to have counsel. That counsel is to be a counsel, as I understand it, represent-Mr. GEOFFRION.
ing the public and the public alone. Therefore I want to have an understanding before this matter goes any further whether this is, bona fide, a movement on behalf of the people to have a counsel appointed to represent them or whether it is not merely a colourable movement for the purpose of adding another counsel who will fortify the ranks of the commission and in that way the ranks of the government. What is the position now? We have a committee of judges, seven of them, of whom four are the appointees of the government, men in sympathy with the government and with the government alone, interested, as far as politics are concerned, to try and come to the conclusion that this matter has been all moonshine, that there is nothing in it. Now we have the majority of the judges who are to try the government supporters of the government, we have the commission in close alliance with the government employing a counsel at the public expense of course, and without consulting the minority of the committee, and we have a well organized staff, as far as political warfare is concerned in the personnel of the commission and we have all the staff of engineers, who are interested in showing that there is nothing wrong and as against that we have only three members of the opposition to watch that whole matter and try in the interests of the public to elicit the real facts of the case. I therefore, feel that this is only another gold brick added to what we had when this matter was inaugurated a little while ago. If we are not to have a clear and definite understanding that, as has been done on former occasions, the minority of the committee, the persons who are interested in bringing home these charges, the Conservative members of the committee if you like, shall have the selection of the counsel who shall represent the public on this occasion. I have no use for it and no faith in it. I want to make no bones about the matter at all, I want to say that when I make this statement I am not assuming, as I might be quite justified in assuming, that the majority of the committee will force upon the minority. A counsel in in whom the minority have not confidence, but I claim as a distinct right and by reason of precedents which have occurred before as well as upon principle, that the minority necessarily in this case represents the public and the public interests and that the selection should be left absolutely in their hands. Although I might have confidence in this committee, that the majority when we meet would accord to the minority what is manifestly their right and what is manifestly only consistent with fair play, yet as having a public duty

to discharge, I do not feel that I would be right in taking any risks in this matter because we know that risks can be taken in a matter of this kind. Therefore, to put the matter beyond any question, I shall take the responsibility of asking that the responsibility for this shall be placed where it ought to be placed, on the government; I shall ask that the government will intimate at this stage, in order that I shall not have to press this matter to extremities, that the preference of the minority of the committee shall be acceded to and in order that the government may have an opportunity of taking a definite position in this matter, and without referring to cases which have been before parliament on previous occasions and which have been dealt with in the committees, I shall move to amend the motion by adding thereto the following words:
It is further ordered that the members of the opposition upon the said committee shall have the right to select the counsel so to be appointed, and that such counsel shall be instructed to protect the interests of the people of Canada in the said investigation.

As a member of the committee that was appointed to investigate the charges in question I am very much surprised indeed at the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). The report which has been presented to the House is one which was adopted to-day by the committee unanimously. It was not suggested then by my hon. friend that there should be any amendment to the report. The motion was made, the committee was not even divided upon it and by the unanimous voice of that committee .the report was made which was presented to the House to-day and which the House has been asked to concur in by the motion of the chairman of the committee. It seems to me that it is a reflection on the committee, a suggestion that they are not competent to appoint counsel who are entitled to the confidence of the public in dealing with this matter. It is a rather singular reversal of the usual order of things that a minority should govern instead of a majority. If the majority of that committee is not entitled to the confidence of the community, to the confidence of this House, I would submit to my hon. friend that his motion ought to be to substitute others for the majority of the committee instead of reversing the established order of things, that the majority shall rule.

The motion made in the committee that an application should be made to the House for authority to appoint counsel to represent the public was
declared to be, so far as it went, satisfactory, and so it was. It was in that sense that we accepted it. It would not have been proper to begin the discussion of who the counsel should be, or exactly how he should be appointed by the committee, until we had got permission from this House to make an appointment. I am surprised at the hon. gentleman making an objection of this kind. One would imagine he thought that the minority of that committee would be quite safe in allowing this appointment to go to the vote of the committee as a whole, trusting that the majority would accept our suggestion. Anybody who has been present at the committee so far knows that the hon. gentleman who has made this motion (Mr. Lennox), is strictly within his rights, and is only acting with common prudence. If the hon. gentleman who has just spoken felt that the suggestion made was a reasonable one, all he would have to do was to say: We concede that much to the minority, we regret that they did not ask for it before. The hon. gentleman has not yet given the slightest intimation of his own opinion as to whether or not we ought to nominate that counsel. What are the facts? The committee met and they notified the commission to appear be-for them, as well as Mr. Lumsden. The commission appeared there at once by counsel, a very eminent counsel of Montreal, paid out of the public purse. He is the counsel of tire commissioners, and if anybody is charged, or if there is anybody to whom misconduct has been imputed, it is the commission. They, through engineers appointed by themselves, are charged with misconduct of so grave a character that the Prime Minister was compelled to move for a committee upon it. What does this gentleman tell us. He rises and says: I represent the public, we are going to investigate these grave charges reflecting upon the commission, and I, their counsel, am going to act for the public in the investigation. Could anything be more ridiculous, more monstrous as a matter of public interest. The gentleman said to the committee that the instructions of the Commission were to probe this matter to the bottom, and he would do his duty! We have, in days gone by, heard counsel employed, apparently on behalf of the public, make such assertions and we know what was the result, we know that the inquiry, instead of being probed to the bottom, was stifled, and while I' do not for a moment impute any thing against the character or probity of Mr. Smith, I do say it is a ridiculous thing to think that in an investigation of this character involving the reputation of the government

who appointed this commission, and of the commission who appointed the engineers charged with misconduct, involving all their positions, that the Commission should appoint counsel to act for the public, and that the majority of a committee named by the government should appoint ing counsel on the other side. I am talking to men of knowledge, business men and politicians who sit on both sides of this House. I ask them if they seriously think that a counsel appointed by the majority of that political committee, politicians on both sides, four on one side and three on the other, will be a counsel who will probe to the bottom questions involving the reputation of the government?
I am surprised that the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke) would stand up in his place and for a moment give colour to such a pretense as that the majority on the committee have any right to make such an appointment. The hon. gentleman knows that we have questions of this kind again and again in committees, and that there is as straight a party vote as there would be in this House. We have on this committee-^three on one side and three on the other, the chairman's casting vote deciding the question. It is a foregone conclusion when we go to a vote how it will result, and we must either agree to the proposition made or there will be a v(te and the vote is sure to go against us. Why do these gentlemen object? Is it a matter of courtesy or ceremony, that we have not been sufficiently ceremonious to these gentlemen in asking them to let us appoint counsel? We ask here in the House that we, as the minority who are concerned in probing this thing, and are determined to probe it to the bottom, shall name the counsel who shall nrosecute the investigation, and that we shall not have appointed another counsel, like Mr. Smith, who acts only for the commission. We do not doubt that an able man would be appointed by the majority, but we would like to know that the man had his heart in the work as well as his head. We want this thing probed no matter what the consequences may be, no matter who may suffer. We have made no charge. This committee was moved not by this side of the House, but by the Prime Minister. Surely he did not mean to go through a farce in moving for this investigation to be not con' tent with a majority of the committee, but must also appoint all the counsel. Through the commission they have appointed Mr. Smith, K.O., and the majority of the committee wish to appoint Mr. Brown or some one else, and we will be told: Oh, you agreed that counsel should be appointed. you have counsel, this is a thorough investigation and the public is Mr. BARKER.
represented. I would have expected the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke) to he the first man to stand up and say: We will hear counsel, we will let you nominate them because you are the attacking parties in this , committee. Does any one doubt that the majority of that committee are on the defensive? Are they not anxious, by every means in their power, to find a verdict of ' not guilty ' as against the commission and against the engineers? Every man on both sides of the House knows that is the fact.
I do not wish to occupy another moment of the time of the House on this question. I say that hon. gentlemen on the other side who refuse this reasonable proposition, that we who are the investigators in fact should have the nomination of the counsel who is to conduct the investigation, are supporting the government in an evasion of the inquiry.
House divided on amendment, Mr. Lennox.

House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the second reading of Bill (No. 95), respecting the naval service of Canada, the proposed amendment of Mr. Borden thereto, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Monk.

When the House adjourned yesterday, I was considering the resolution unanimously passed by this House last March. If you examine carefully each clause of that resolution, you will find that the position taken to-day by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is absolutely consistent with every one of those clauses. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition does call for speedy organization, for co-operation, for close relations with the British navy and for active participation. I also contend that the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has gone back on every principle embodied in that resolution. Sir, the Bill before us is not a policy of speedy organization, but one of delay; it is not a policy of co-operation, but one which makes co-operation absolutely impossible; it is not a policy of naval service in close relation with the British navy, but a policy designed to keep our fleet of vessels separate from the British navy; it is not a policy of active participation, but one of useless inactivity; it is not a policy to render our commerce and the empire more secure, but a policy of graft and ingratitude, a policy to breed another flock of political vultures to add to those that have followed in the wake of this government since 1896 and have grown fat on what they have_ stolen from the people of Canada. This is not an imperial policy; it is not a Canadian policy, but it is, in my estimation, a policy of rank and brazen hypocrisy which waves the British flag before the eyes of the Canadian people as the talisman of liberty and plots the disintegration of the empire behind its protecting folds. Never in the history of the British empire has any statesman occupied so pitiable a position of weakness and vaccil-lation as that now occupied by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads this House. It is difficult to follow

the right hon. gentleman in his political gymnastics on any great question, but, on this question, I contend he has well earned the title of champion political lightning change artist of the continent of America.
What has been his course? Speaking in this House last March, the right hon. gentleman gave pledges of sympathy and loyal support. Last November, he said that not a ship should go without the consent of parliament. Last December he modified that somewhat by saying that we might help if England were severely pressed. Early this month, he said that if England is at war, Canada is at war. And later in the present month he modified that again by saying that he meant that when England was at war Canada was at war, inasmuch as Canada formed part of the empire and was liable to attack when England was at war, but he did not mean that Canada was necessarily involved in taking part in all England's wars. I was somewhat amused, the other evening, at the effort of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) to reconcile the positive and negative statements of his leader. Any such evolutions and contortions as the hon. member went through in order to reconcile the two positions of his leader would give a snake lumbago. On this great question, involving the future destiny of Canada and the empire, we see the premier of this country suspended in mid air. like Mahomet's spirit between heaven and hell and fit for neither place, wobbling about like a Chinese kite answering to the sentiments of whatever popular audience he happens to be - addressing-one day uttering sentiments for the ears of British Canadians, and furnishing headlines for such papers as the Toronto ' Globe,' the next day uttering sentiments for those Trench Canadians whom he has carefully schooled to look in the direction of his highest aspirations. Sir, the right hon. gentleman has become an expert in the manipulation of the English language. The people of Canada have become somewhat accustomed to the right hon. gentleman's lingual inconsistencies; but on this great question I think the people of Canada would like from the premier of this country, definite, clear-cut and unequivocal statements. The right hon. gentleman, speaking a few days ago, and referring to the conquest of Canada by Wolfe in 1759, made use of these words:
My ancestors lost on that occasion, but it simply transferred their allegiance from one sovereign to another. They lost the battle, but they did not lose their independence, their liberty, their rights and privileges; and to-day the sun in his daily career does not shed his light upon any people on the face of the earth enjoying more liberty than my fellow countrymen of French extraction. And my last words to the doubters is that

freedom is worth fighting for and worth dying for.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that these words are true. And yet, Sir, time and again it has been impressed upon us in this House that there is an anti-imperial sentiment in the province of Quebec which has to be reckoned with when any great political question comes before this House and country. There is no getting around this, and there is no use in mincing words in dealing with it. We have heard it stated in this House within the last few days that if one should undertake to criticise an estimate for a wharf or a post office in the province of Quebec he is liable to be misrepresented in that province as being antagonistic to the French Canadian people. We know that, time and again, we have been cautioned to be very careful how we considered any question on which the people of Lower Canada have an opinion which differs from ours. In the consideration of the French treaty it was almost as much as a man's position was worth to express an adverse criticism, no matter how honestly he might held that view, for fear of being misrepresented as an Anglo-Saxon bigot. In the case of the hanging of Louis Riel, who was judged to be a traitor, it was represented as due to his French origin. In the matter of dealing with the Manitoba school question, the people of this country were given to understand by one leader that Manitoba must submit to the will of Quebec, while the other leader took advantage of the position to gain power in order that he might use that power to coerce the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and, subsequently as has been made apparent to everybody in this country, has given Manitoba to understand that she must remain the ' postage stamp province ' until she is willing to bend the knee to the will of Quebec. While we recognize the fact that there are people in this Dominion of French origin, I wish to remind hon. gentlemen opposite, and I do it in all kindness, that there are also people of English, Irish, Scotch and Welsh origin, and that the interests of the English-speaking people must receive more consideration in the future than_ they have in the past. I maintain that the English-speaking portion of this country has been held up before the eyes of the world by the premier and his delegates at different imperial conferences as being indifferent and callous to the calls of their kindred across the sea. That is the only conclusion we can come to from the position taken by the Tight hon. First Minister and other delegates at different imperial conferences. It seems that the uppermost thought in the mind of the government is: What will Quebec say or think? Ontario and the other provinces, they seem to conclude, can be relied upon I 130J
to be fooled as usual with a few sentenceshaving an imperial ring, but really as empty as sounding brass. I have not one word to say against the French Canadians of this country. I believe they are an energetic and intelligent people. I, myself, think that they are an exceptionally intelligent people, because, Sir, if what the hon. member for Hochelaga said yesterday, that there is no feeling of disloyalty among the French Canadians of Quebec is correct, I say it speaks very highly for the intelligence of the people of that province, for if there is no feeling of disloyalty in the province of Quebec it is not for lack of teaching by hon. gentlemen opposite. Battleships and cannon are very necessary implements of war, but a country's strength does not depend on these alone. It does not depend on these so much as on the men behind the guns. We cannot measure the military and naval strength of Canada by the calibre of our cannon or by the number of Bristols. But, if we are honest with ourselves and honest with the people of the country, we have to take into consideration, in viewing this question, the sentiments not only of Canada as a whole, but of each part of Canada.
The hon. member for Hochelaga challenged any one in this House to say that there is a feeling of disloyalty in Quebec. I do not like to use the word disloyalty, but I do believe we have ample evidences in this House in the expressions which have fallen from the lips of different speakers that there is in the province of Quebec an anti-British, or, if you like it better, an anti-imperial sentiment. I propose to deal with that matter squarely and to place the blame for that sentiment, which I do not consider in the interests of Canada, where it justly belongs. Is there an hon. member in this House who will deny my assertion that separation from the empire is preached in the province of Quebec? Is there an hon. member in this House who will deny my assertion that public money of the province of Quebec has been used to buy books to disseminate such doctrines in that province? I will challenge any man in this House.	I
will challenge any man in the piovince of Quebec to deny that assertion.	I
say that that separation from the empire has been preached in the province of Quebec not only on the platform but through subsidized books.
What book?

The hon. gentleman asks me what book, and I will tell him. The following statement was'made by the Winnipeg 'Telegram' some time ago A
The Quebec element opposed to aiding the nary of Great Britain, is also the element which talks seriously of the disintegration of confederation.

The late Mr. Tardivel's book, ' Pour la Patrie/ advocating the organization of a French republic on the northeast corner of the American continent, which book was designed to imbue the rising generation in Quebec with the idea of separation from the English-speaking portion of Canada, is still the subject of very general comment east and west. Three hundred dollars was spent by the Quebec government to distribute this book as prizes among the children of the schools of Quebec.
Where is the wrong-doing?

There may not appear to be any wrong from the hon. gentleman's standpoint and in that respect he and 1 will have to differ, but from the way I look upon it, it is decidedly wrong not only for any man in this House but for any person in this country to preach the separation of Canada from the empire. In my estimation the wrong is accentuated when the legislature of the province of Quebec votes, as it did vote, $300 of public money to buy these books to scatter that treason throughout the province of Quebec. The hon. gentleman may not see any wrong in that but I do.
I asked what was the wrong, because I have read that book. The true meaning of that book is not that which is given to it by the 'Telegram'.
Will the hon. gentleman rise in his place in this House and tell us that that book does not advocate the establishment of a French republic in Quebec?
Not at all. That is only the workings of the hon. gentleman's imagination.

I assert that $300 of the public money of the province of Quebec was voted for that purpose, and the proof of my assertion will be found in the Votes and Proceedings of the legislature of Quebec for December 3, 1896. Nor is that the only instance. Mr. Tardival's idea has been elaborated by Rev. Father Hamon who advocates the formation of a federation of the French Canadian societies of Canada and the United States. Father Hamon's work received the approval of Archbishop Taschereau. At chapter 18 of the book you will find these words:
See what will happen when the French 'Canadian race shall have completely occupied the space relatively restricted and found between the north shore of the St. Lawrence and the American boundary, that which we call the eastern townships. It will not probably take more than another generation to accomplish this work. Then the grand invasion (of the republic), will commence. When the French Canadians shall have ar-Mr. EDWARDS.
rived in mass at the American boundary line they will find more than half a million of their compatriots awaiting them who have the Canadian parish organized as absolutely as in Quebec, and are very decided, while discharging their duties loyally as citizens, to remain everywhere French. The French Canadians in the United States will soon be too numerous and influential for any political party, whatever it might wish to do, to dare to dispute their privileges. The American union is too big to be managed successfully. It is within the range of the possible that there will be a break-up when Quebec, New Brunswick, Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and, possibly, eastern Ontario, will constitute a distinct republic, French and Roman Catholic, Quebec giving a spirit and character to the new republic. Thus it may be, in the order of Providence, that there will be regained, by the observance of nature's laws of increase, and religious fidelity and love of country that which, in September, 1759, the sword wrested from the French Canadians on the Heights of Abraham.
I have not one word to say against the aspirations of Father Hamon to extend his religion as far as he possibly can. That is a worthy aspiration from h'is standpoint. But I do object to the preaching of any doctrine in any part of Canada which means the disintegration of this country and the separation of it from the British empire.
Will my hon. friend allow me one question. Will he tell me in what year the book he refers to was published by the Quebec government?
I have already stated it was in 1896.

I may say that in the year 1896, in the province of Quebec, the party in power was the Conservative party; the party which is to-day led in the province of Quebec by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.

Now, Mr. Speaker, that is just about what I expected. I stand here to say that I do not care whether it was done by the Conservative party in Quebec, or by the Liberal party in Quebec, I object to this as un-Canadian.
My hon. friend will not find that in the Liberal ranks.

I was just as well aware as the hon. member was, what party was in power in Quebec when that book was prepared. This seems so interesting to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that I want to give them a little more of it. Let us see what some of their great politicians and statesmen have done; let us see the stand that the Hon. Mr. Mercier took in that province. I might remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. Beland)

that, Mr. Mercier was one of the lights of the Liberal party. He was premier of Quebec from 1887 to 1891, and he was an advocate of cutting the tie with Britain and of declaring Quebec a great French Canadian nation, to which the Canadians who had gone to the New England states would return. Let me give you a quotation or two from his great Sohmer Park speech. On that occasion Mr. Mercier said:
Taking everything into account French Canadians owe nothing to England. If they had prospered, it was in spite of England, not because of her, and if England had done them any good, it had also done them still greater harm. On the whole we owe nothing to England, and we may separate ourselves from her when the majority constitutionally decides to do so without any pangs of conscience and without any shedding of tears. I advise my compatriots to ask for independence for four leading reasons. From necessity, from patriotism, from the natural advantages of independence, because we are capable of existing as an independent people. As a free man, on this free soil of Canada, I defend The sacred cause of my compatriots, whatever may be their race or their religious belief, and I demand for all, men, women, and children, colonial emanciption and liberty. You have colonial dependence; I offer you independence. You have ruin and misery; I offer you fortune and prosperity. You are now only a colony, ignored by the entire world; I offer you the opportunity of becoming a great people, respected and known by all free nations. Men, women and children, it is for you to choose. You may remain slaves in the colonial state, or become independent and free, in the midst of other peoples, who, by their all-powerful voices, are inviting you to the banquet of the nations.
Mr. Mercier was not Prime Minister of Quebec in that year.
I did not say he was.
He was turned down by his province for that language.
I said that Mr. Mercier was a very prominent Canadian.
Not at that time.

Oh, yes, he was prominent even at that time. I say he was sufficiently prominent that he in the course of time occupied the position of premier _ of the province of Quebec from which position he was turned out by the people of Quebec in 1891. Later on, when addressing a meeting of the French Canadians of New England, at Fall River, he said:
You who were driven out of the province of Quebec by the constitution and non-progressive policy of that country, as she is ruled by the English, have been more than able to hold your own in another country which is a free republic. I appeal to you to always be ready ' to assist your
compatriots in Canada who are struggling for liberty; and the only thing wanted to release them from their present bondage is independence.'

Mr. Mercier is the greatest Canadian since the time of Papineau. I believe with Mr. Mercier, and I am here to make him prevail.

It is nothing more nor less than public endorsation and approval of one who taught sedition and scattered the seeds of treason. That is my position and I object to that sort of thing. You do not know what you are talking about.

I say to my hon. friends that it would be as consistent for them to erect a statue to Louis Riel, because although he did incite two rebellions he had at least the courage to undergo himself the risk that he induced other people to take. Now, Mr. Speaker, did the right hon. gentleman who leads this House exert his powerful influence at that time to try and stop that sort of thing. In Toronto, a short time ago, the right hon. gentleman said: That if he had any success in this country he owed it to the fact that he had told his compatriots in Queoec to lay their prejudices and preferences on the altar of their country. But let us follow the course of the right hon. gentleman and see about that. On the 22nd of November, 1885, there was an immense gathering assembled on the Champ de Mars, Montreal, for the purpose of protesting against the execution of Louis Riel. At that meeting a telegram was read from the open and undisguised foes of Great Britain in New York city. That telegram read:
We tender you our warmest sympathy and assure you of our earnest support againsc Orange brutality and English tyranny.
(Signed) J. B. MURPHY,

Did the right hon. gentleman, the leader of this government, arise to protest against that? Did he rise and protest, and appeal to the people there assembled to lay their prejudices and preferences on the altar of their country? No, Mr. Speaker, but as soon as the cheers that had greeted this telegram had subsided, the right hon. gentleman got up and said. If I had been on the banks of the Saskatchewan when the revolt broke out, I would have taken up arms against the government. Is this an isolated instance of such expressions on the part of the premier of this country? No. The very next year after that when he had full time to consider and deliberate, the very next year at Chambly he repeated that assertion and added:
We are now on the classic ground of Canadian liberty. In the graveyards of this country are to be found the bones of those who were not afraid co face British bullets.
Mr. Speaker, I have no faith in the Prime Minister of this country when he gets up in Toronto and tells the people theTe, and tells the country through the press, that he has told the people of his province as patriots to lay their prejudices and preferences on the altar of their country. I say that his whole career shows an entirely different course. If you follow the right hon. gentleman's career a little further what do you find him doing? Four or five years later you find him trying to persuade the people of Canada to adopt a policy which Mr. E. ROY.
Edward Blake said meant nothing more or less than annexation. And, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman at that time did not seem to be at all concerned about Canadian autonomy either. In 1892, page 1142 'Hansard', he said:
I hold out to my fellow-countrymen the idea of independence.
Again, 'Hansard', page 1144, he said:
I have again and again repeated that the goal of my aspiration is the independence of Canada.
In Boston about the same time he was declaring that it was a fatal mistake to make allegiance-that is British allegiance -the basis of trade; that the present position of Canada to Great Britain could not last, and that separation must take place; that the conduct of Canada and of Great Britain -had been unworthy of the civilization of Canada and Great Britain during the American civil war. And, mind you, Mr. Speaker, that in face of the fact that thousands of Canadians assisted the North in that war and that our records contain the published thanks of the American government to the government of Canada for the wise and neutral course they pursued on that occasion. And, as to the position of Great Britain in connection with that historical period, let me give you the words of the right hon. W. E. Gladstone, who in writing to an American friend said:
I can state that the British government never at any time dealt with the subject of recognizing the southern states in your great civil war, excepting when it learned the proposition of the Emperor Napoleon III., and declined to entertain that proposition without qualification, hesitation, delay or assent.
The whole political career of the Prime Minister is marked by utterances designed to weaken Canadian respect for and loyalty to the motherland.
Will you allow me a question? Do you think that all French-Canadians to-day are not loyal to the British Crown?
Mr. Speaker, I stated some time ago, very clearly and distinctly-

Just sit down now; I stated very clearly and distinctly that I accepted the position taken last night by the member for Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet) when he said that the people of the province of Quebec were not disloyal. I repeat, Sir, that, by the leader of this government history has been perverted; I say that British diplomacy has been misrepresented by him on more than one occasion. I am not going to enter into details with Tegard to British diplomacy. But, Sir, I believe the time will come when British statesmen will receive more of credit and less of adverse criticism for their diplomacy in connection with Canadian affairs than they have received in times past. I want to say this more:	That it comes with very
bad grace from any member from the province of Quebec to attack British diplomacy, because the people of the province of Quebec have more reason to be grateful to British diplomacy than any other people in the Dominion. I say, Sir, it comes with exceeding bad grace from the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, for. Sir, if Canadian diplomacy as represented by the right hon. gentleman himself and his party had succeeded in 1891 we would not have any Canada to-day-we would be an annex of the United States. When trouble broke out in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand responded with alacrity; Canada held back. Now, supposing in the case of the item that came up in the House the other day for a vote of $50,000 for the sufferers in Paris, any hon. gentleman m this House had got up and opposed it, saying:	I do not believe that there is any

Why all the armaments if we are not to have war, and why fight for England.

These carbines, these guns will be used by the electors. They would send our children to Africa, to Asia, from where they would never return.

Now, as regards this question of emergency, let us see for a moment the position of the British government in that regard. The British government, in March, 1909, had in their programme four Dreadnoughts and possibly four more if, on considering the state of affairs, these latter four were found necessary. Now, Sir, add to that, some words taken from the speech from the Throne delivered no later than last Monday:
The requirements of the naval defence of the empire have made it necessary to prepose a substantial increase in the cost of the navy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that when we on this side of the House claim that there is an emergency impending, we do not deserve to be styled ' scaremongers.' But, if you would have even further proof, allow me to give you still another authority, and one who, I have no doubt, will appeal to every hon. member on the other side of the House-no less an authority than the right hon. premier of this country. Speaking in this House last March, the right hon. gentleman uttered these words:
This brings us to something which is in the air at present and which no British subject can ignore. For a hundred years and more the naval supremacy of Great Britain has been unquestioned-nay more, British supremacy on the seas has been so absolute that no one supposed it could ever be disputed. But this is an age when events happen very fast. We have learned lately that the foremost military power of the world at present is contemplating perhaps to cope with Great Britain on the high seas. We have, perhaps, reason to believe, as we have just been told that Germany is building more ships than Great Britain and building them more rapidly. Possibly there is a conclusion to be drawn from this, and the only conclusion is that Germany intends some time to do with Great Britain on the high seas what she has done with France on land. Everybody knows, it is a matter of history that Prussia had for years been silently preparing to cope with France, which, up to that time, had been the greatest military nation in the world, that Prussia waited its opportunity, and when that opportunity came, delivered a mortal blow. If it be true then that Germany is organizing on the seas, no British subject can afford to be indifferent to the prospect.
Well, Sir, we on this side are not indifferent to that prospect, but I contend that hon. gentlemen opposite, in the present policy, are indifferent to- the prospect referred to by their leader. And, if you take these words of the premier and place them before any audience in the Dominion of Canada and ask the members- of that audience what these words mean, I believe that every man will say that these words were meant to indicate- that the situation was grave, and that the premier apprehended danger to Britain and to the empire from Germany. And, if any man in that audience should need anything further to confirm him in that view, he could take these further words of the premier, spoken a little later on the occasion already referred to:
Vigilance and eternal vigilance must be the watchword to-day, not only in England, but in Canada and every other part of the British empire.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, including their leader, now tell us that there is no emergency, and that we are ' scaremongers,' who believe that there is an emergency impending. Sir, not even Robert Blatchford himself has used language more significant or more pregnant with alarm than that used by the leader of this government last March. If there is no cause for apprehension on our part, what is the necessity for the plunge into this new policy? If no danger is to he apprehended from Germany, why not submit this policy-involving, as it does, the expenditure during the .next four or five years of $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 and, in the near future, an expenditure running into hundreds of millions- to the mature consideration and decision of the people of Canada?
Well, Sir, will this proposed flotilla of unarmoured cruisers add anything to the strength of the British navy or be an effective and complete defence for Canada itself? Is it not true that we shall have still to depend on England to protect us from the vital thrust of war, while we toot our tin horns and provide a toy fleet against possible and improbable pin pricks. We pretend to assume insignificant minor risks from stray raiding cruisers which we very well know would not dare to take the risk cf going three thousand miles from their

base of supplies, but we leave it to England to provide our real protection. If England provides such protection, no large vessels can get at us. This government is assuming that Great Britain will still Tetain her general command of the seas. If the right hon. Prime Minister had any intention of strengthening the empire on the seas, he would have supplemented the British navy where the British navy needed supplementing. Where is the British navy weakest, according to the expression of opinion of her best statesmen? It is relatively weakest in Dreadnoughts. And where is it strongest? Figures show to us that it is relatively strongest in cruisers. And I contend that if there were any real desire on the part of this government to strengthen the British navy, they would give assistance where the British navy was relatively weakest, and not where it was relatively strongest. Meanwhile population increased, the West made further leaps in the way of development, the volume of trade doubled, new railways were built in ajl directions; Canada, in short, after being for a long time a mere colony evolved into a nation in the eyes of the world, enjoying new privileges and bearing new responsibilities.
It was then that one of the leaders of the Conservative party in this House, the hon. member for North Toronto inserted in the order paper the following proposal:
That in the opinion of this House, in view of her great and varied resources, of her geographical position and national environments, and of that spirit of self help and self respect which alone befits a strong and growing people, Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great seaports.
When that resolution was discussed, that is on March 9th, 1909, its lack of precise meaning prevented the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition from agreeing to it, especially for fear it might put our country under the necessity of a direct contribution to the British exchequer, a contingency which did not appear acceptable to either party. So, it was thrown aside by mutual agreement, and another, of which I need quote a part only to the House, substituted therefor. For the purpose of this debate, it will suffice to quote the following paragraph which is essential:
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last Imperial Conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and. the peace of the world.'
That resolution was discussed, but when I say discussed, I wish to be well understood. Not a single voice was raised against it, comments from both sides of i h. House were invariably favourable. Where were the men who are to-day opposing the government, and why did they not raise their voices in condemnation of the proposal? And if they did not wish to speak out, why did they not vote against the measure, which in principle and in its essentia] features is the same as that submitted to parliament to-day. It is of primary importance that the people of this country,



and particularly of the province of Quebec, should be made aware that it was then unanimously adopted, witnout even the hon. member for Jacques Cartier dissenting.
Now, I ask again, what is it that carried unanimously at that time? In the first place, the asserting of the unswerving fidelity of Canada towards the mother country; in the second place the disproval of the principle of a direct money contribution to the British exchequer; in the third place, our hearty approval of the establishment of a national navy. So then, the colonial conference held in London in 1902, the stand taken by the Canadian parliament in 1903; the general elections in 1904 and 1908; the resolution unanimously adopted by parliament in 1909, these circumstances, it would seem, are more than sufficient to set aside the contention of those who allege that the question has never been brought up in the past and should take the form of a plebiscite.
Besides, what would be the outcome of a plebiscite on a question of that kind? Have those of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec who advocate a plebiscite pon- dered over the probable results of a consultation of the people? Is it not selfevident that the Anglo-Saxon blood would be stirred ur>
by those who have accepted the tenets of the policy of imperialism as advocated by Mr. Chamberlain, and that through the kindling of prejudices by expert hands through the intense political feeling aroused, and appeals to racial and religious uassions, a majority of electors might pronounce in favour of the nefarious principle of a money contribution to the British admiralty. I, for one, would fear having recourse to a plebiscite, as it would result in dangerous appeals to prejudice, and thereby be a menace to the maintenance of our institutions.
A plebiscite, I readily conceive, would afford extremists a fine opportunity for abetting popular passions, awakening old racial enmities, setting up one against the other the two great races living in harmony in this country from the national and religious standpoint. It is hoped that thereby the two sections of the Conservative party would affect a step in advance, by representing in Quebec the Prime Minister as sacrificing Canada to England, while in Ontario and the west, he would be held up as the sworn foe of England, because the Bill gives Canada control over its navy. As a matter of fact, it should not be forgotten that this is the very reason given by the leader of the opposition for demanding a plebiscite.
The stand taken by the leader of the opposition should not cause too much surprise. It is one among his many shiftings of which we have had the spectacle in the Mr. BELAND.
course of the last year. Indeed, we have seen a moment ago that on March 29th, 1909, that is less than a year ago, the House declared unanimously in favour of the establishment of a Canadian navy. At that date,, the leader freely chosen by all sections of the party opposite, not even excepting the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, proclaimed the principle of selfgovernment in the matter of the navy as well as in matters of militia, urged the government to build forthwith, and to carry to rapid completion, a national naval service, and repudiated the idea of a direct money contribution to the British exchequer. On January 12, 1910, about a month ago, from his seat in this House, he spoke as follows:
It has been suggested that instead of the organization of a Canadian naval force, there should be a system of annual contributions from this country to the mother country; and I am free to admit that, from the strategical point of view, that I would be inclined to agree with the view of the admiralty that that would be the best way for the great selfgoverning dominions of the empire to make their contributions. But, Sir, from a' constitutional and political standpoint, I am opposed to it, for many reasons.
As all may see, he had not yet performed that famous somersault, that most laughable bout-face ever recorded in the parliamentary annals of this country. But after a stormy eaucas during which, if rumour is to be credited, the Quebec Conservatives and those from the English-speaking provinces, came to hands, he emerged with a new policy. Then, Sir, he discards all his great principles hardly twelve months old; what he now advocates is not the building of a national navy with wisdom and prudence, kept under the control of the Dominion government and parliament. Not by any means. To-day, he comes before parliament, and in the name of the great Conservative party, he says: Let us give-125,000,000 to England, -as a gift pure and simple; let us let the country be invited to pay an amount equivalent to three dollars for each man, woman and child; let us make that gift to England, without reserving the right of ever requiring that these ships built with our cash will be used primarily for the protection of our coasts and our trade. That is on the part of the leader of the opposition an overt step in the direction of imperial federation and the complete abandonment of our autonomy. I, for one, shall oppose, with all my might that dangerous proposal of a money contribution.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier demands a plebiscite, and his leader demands the same thing, but is it with the same object in view? Let us see. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier, if I understand

him aright, is of opinion that the government measure effects a radical change in our relations with Great Britain; and in support of this contention, he points to clause 18 of the Bill which enables the Governor in Council, that is the Dominion government, to put in a case of emergency the Canadian navy at the disposal of His Majesty. To my mind, that reservation which is incorporated in the Bill on behalf of the Dominion government, is the mere conferring of a discretionary power, is nothing but a further assertion of our autonomy, especially if read in conjunction with clause 19 which states that no such decision will take effect unless it be ratified by the Dominion parliament, that is, by the representatives of the people. In the opinion of the hon. member (Mr. Monk), there is no necessity for protecting our coasts, our sea ports. To his mind, the situation in Canada has not changed for the last twenty years, or within the last decade. To his mind, our sea-going trade is too insignificant to require any protection on our part. His policy is one of expectation, but not one such as is termed in medical practice,
' armed expectation,' but an expectation without preparation or foresight. Should ha have his way, and our trade is harassed at sea, and our vessels loaded with food products sunk by the enemy's warships, our only recourse would be to fold our arms and call on England to protect us. And if England was not in a position to relieve us, her ships being kept busy on the German ocean or in some other quarter, would the hon. member suggest that we invoke the Monroe doctrine, that is to say, the protection of the United States? Surely not, for my hon. friend as a Canadian would be too proud to remain inactive awaiting the protection of a foreign country.
On the other hand, the leader of the opposition, that is to say, the leader of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, would be in favour of a plebiscite, for this reason, that the Bill provides that the proposed navy will remain under the control of the Canadian paliament. He is in favour of a navy, even of a stronger navy than the one proposed, and if he demands a plebiscite, it is with a view of obtaining from the people authority to place it as soon as completed at the entire disposal of the British admiralty. If England and Canada were to be attacked simultaneously, the leader of the opposition is willing that our fleet should be against our will summoned to the mouth of the Thames, the coasts of England, or elsewhere, at the sweet will of the British admiralty. That is a second breach to the principle of autonomy, a second repudiation of his statements of a year ago, of a month ago.
And, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party 1314
is actually identified with the leader of the opposition. It is all very well for the member for Jacques Cartier to seemingly break away from his leader on that question; it is all very well for him to rouse the province of Quebec and acquire cheap popularity; but whenever Sir Wilfrid Laurier relinguishes the reins of power and give3 way before an expression of popular will throughout the Dominion, it is the leader of the opposition who will be summoned to take hold of the government, and the Conservatives of the province of Quebec, who to-day condemn the prime minister on account of his policy of a Canadian navy Kept under our control, would be the first you may be sure, to acclaim Mr. Bordei , though he is in favour of a larger fleet put entirely at the disposal of Great Britain, and besides of paying over a money contribution of $25,000,000.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier may be sure that this old trick will fail as did the others and that the people will understand the duplicity of the Cqnservative party who is attempting to attain office by the worn-out tactics of crying: ' too much ' in Quebec and ' not enough ' in Ontario. The excellent people of Quebec are told: Laurier, your fellow countryman is a traitor, he becoming too English, and in Ontario it is proclaimed that Laurier is disloyal and a traitor to England because he refuses to pay over $25,000,000 in money and to place the Canadian navy unrestrictedly under English control.	_
There exists in the country, both in Quebec and in the English speaking provinces, a party of moderate opinions, rejecting all extremist and dangerous views. This majority has on every important occasion, decided the issue in such manner as the true interests of Canada required. In the present case common issue will prevail against all wild statements, false accusations, insults and denounciations whether they be uttered by ultra loyalists or by demagogues.
The Bill now submitted to parliament is essentially a Canadian measure and the methods of those opposing it are decidedly dangerous from a Canadian point of view. I cannot understand that men of the parliamentary standing of the hon. member for North Toronto and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier should devote themselves to a task calculated to strain the harmonious and friendly relations existing between the two great races who inhabit this country.
The measure is neither extraordinary nor even absolutely new. I say this advisedly, and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who opposes it so strenuously and with so little justification, has admitted it himself. I say that this measure is nothing more than an adaptation to the navy of the Mili-
The hon. member knows quite well that we have no merchant marine.

It is not necessary that we should have a merchant marine of our own to export our produce.
I am appealing now to those hon. members representing agricultural constituencies where the dairy industry is flourishing and who proclaim everywhere that in opposing the present Bill they voice the opinion of the farmers. They owe it to their constituents to vote for the measure. I repeat it, the agricultural class has a paramount interest in the Bill, because agriculture should in the first place be protected; we must act with prudence and foresight so that in case of war the farming community may not suffer. That cannot be done, as the hon. leader of the Conservative party suggests, by giving over $25,000,000 to Great Britain to strengthen her fleet, but by expending a smaller but a sufficient sum for the building of a Canadian navy able to protect our own fishermen, our coasts, our sea ports and the produce of our farms shipped for export.
This is (the weak point in the position of the few Conservative abstainers. My first reason for supporting the measure is that it is essentially Canadian; my second is that the navy so established will 'become an indispensable factor in the protection of our export trade; my third that it will powerfully help to maintain the integrity of the colonial bond with Great Britain.
Going a step further, I believe I will be able to show paramount reasons why French Canadians should support this measure. Canada is a part of the British empire and they have every interest that Britain should maintain her naval supremacy. If the British empire were to be dismembered it would be an evil day for t'he French population of this country, not only from a commercial point of view but also from that of their national and religious life.
The fact that all the British self-governing colonies are adopting a policy similar to ours, and protecting, be it even, for the time being, to a limited extent, coasts that have hitherto been unprotected, will produce a most important moral effect upon any nation that may have hoped to 'be able to annoy Great Britain or weaken her naval prestige, or who may have dreamed of her dismemberment. It is easy to understand that being confronted by the finest navy in the world-I mean the British navy-protecting the sea coast of the North Sea, the Channel and the Atlantic; and also by the colonial navies stationed at the entrance of the respective ports of Canada. Australia, New Zealand and other colonies, those bellicose enemies of the

British empire will speedily assume an attitude of respect, instead of that of aggressiveness which has been theirs of late years, and that British peace which has been maintained on the high seas for over a century, will still prevail. Thus the best means of securing peace seems to be in those defensive measures which we are at present considering.
In my humble opinion no province is more interested than the province of Quebec in the maintenance of the integrity of the British empire. By the beneficial influence of Britain our rights and privileges granted by the British North America Act are protected against the attempts made by demagogues. In the province of Quebec the French Canadian population enjoy the greatest liberty in matters of education and also as to the official use of their language. I know, Mr. Speaker, that those rights are secured to us 'by the constitution and that our constitution is the result of a conference between Canadian statesmen of different races and religions. But should the prestige of *the mother country vanish, should England, after an unsuccessful war, lose the dominion of the seas, that constitution would become a dead letter, and with it the right of using the French language in the parliament of Canada, the privilege of religious instruction in the separate schools of Quebec and Ontario. Have we sufficiently reflected upon the dreadful consequences which might follow the breaking of the bond between Canada and Britain? We would have to choose between independence and annexation to the United States. Independence, apparently the most acceptable alternative, would none the less entail great responsibilities and enormous risks. The risks would consist chiefly in the numerous difficulties to be encountered in inducing the English and Protestant majority, without the preponderant influence of England, to respect the institutions so dear to us. I am quite willing to admit the generous spirit and breadth of view of the English speaking population of Canada, but I would place even greater faith in the protection of England, for since fifty years and more we would seek in vain for any expression of hostility towards us from the lips of a British statesman, of either party, whereas, unfortunately, the same cannot be said of Canada.	_
I know full well that men there will be in the province of Quebec who will say to the people: ' Perish England and her prestige rather than have a Canadian navy; let us have independence rather than a fleet for the protection of our coasts and commerce.' They will say to us that if by the rupture of the British bond our rights as French Canadian and Catholics were threatened, we might fight as fought
our ancestors on the fields of St. Denis, St. Charles and St. Eustache. Those who might be tempted to use such arguments would certainly prove the greatest enemies of the French race in Canada! _
For my part, I declare once again that the political state of ' Independence of Canada ' would endanger the exercise of our religious and national rights. ^ Let us now turn for a moment to our obligations.
If, financially, the establishment of a navy for purposes of protection, as suggested, is too much for our weak shoulders, if there is anything alarming in the expenditure of the twelve or fifteen millions requisite for the establishment of a rudimentary navy composed of four cruisers and a few smaller ships, can we forget that on becoming independent we will lose the protection of the powerful British navy, and that with the hundreds of miles of sea coast on both oceans, we would be obliged to establish a complete one. That would be much more serious. What is the situation of independent nations? Let us take, as examples, some South American republics. Brazil with a population of 17,000,000 has a navy of 15 battleships; Chili, with a population of 34 millions, has seven battleships; Argentina, with a population of 7 millions, has nine battleships and cruisers. Take the small independent countries of Europe: Holland, with a population of 6 millions, has seventeen cruisers; Sweden, with 7$ millions, fifteen battleships; Denmark, with 24 millions, 9 battleships.
We find that all those countries, with populations smaller than that of Canada, with the exception of Brazil, have much more powerful navies than that contemplated for Canada; the Bill before the House provides for the building of four cruisers and of some tornedo boats.
I remember having read quite recently a speech delivered at the Monument National, Montreal, in direct opposition to the idea of a national navy, by an eminent speaker well known in this House, Mr. Bourassa. In his speech, he developeu this strange contention that Canada, in case of danger, might apply for protection to the United States and require the application of the Monroe doctrine to our case. I humblv submit that for a country lute Canada to rely upon the protection of its neighbour would be a position of the deepest disgrace. It would mean something more than disgrace. . Does anybody suppose that the United States would consent to a breach of neutrality towards any enemy of England without requiring compensation? Certainly not, and the compensation, m this case, would take the form of territorial and trade concessions; perhaps it might also affect our allegiance.	. .	.
From a national and religious point ot view the annexation of Canada to the

United States would be almost as disastrous 1>
the province of Quebec as independence. It will be immediately seen that the French population, instead of being in a proportion of two to five as in Canada, would stand in the pronortion of one to thirty in the United States. We would be delivered up to the almost irresistible assimilating power of the American people. Americans would never permit the use of any language but English in Congress. It is quite reasonable to suppose that no exception would be made in favour of the province of Quebec as to education in the public schools. Annexation also would entail taxation for the support of the United States navy-one of the most powerful in the world- and such taxation would be much heavier than _ any that may be imposed for the creation and maintenance of a navy under the present Bill.
It is clear, therefore, that irom a financial point of view as well as from commercial, national and religious considerations, we have every interest in firmly dismissing all idea of independence or annexation; nay more, that we should be ready to submit to heavy sacrifices for the maintenance of the British bond.
Mgr. Plessis understood this when, in 1807, he said to the Catholic population of Quebec: 'You have understood that your dearest interests are inseparable from those of Great Britain.' He also said that ' his flock would be unworthy of the name of Catholics and Canadians if they showed disloyalty or even indifference in the accomplishment of their duty as subjects devoted to their sovereign's interests and defenders of their country.'
The same advice was given at different times by Bishop Panet, by Bishops Signay and Lartigue, in 1837-8, by Bishops Baili-argeon and Tache, and later by Archbishop Begin, of Quebec, who some years ago, declared in a sermon delivered in a cathedral of France: ' We are happy to live under the British flag and our country is essentially n land of freedom.'
As I do not wish to make my speech too lengthy, I will now close with the remark that in this matter the Liberal party has avoided extremes; the proposal submitted is moderate and consists in a Canadian naval establishment calculated to protect our coasts and cities, our fishermen and *our foreign trade.
The Navy Bill now before the House is the result of eight years of study; it provides for an exclusively Canadian navy, inasmuch as it will be built in Canada, that all the necessary expenditures will be paid into the hands of the Canadian people and that the whole will be under the control of the Canadian parliament.
A plebiscite would become the occasion of unwise apeals, would inevitably result Mr. BELAND
m rousing the English-speaking population, which holds the majority in the country, against the province of Quebec, thus forming an English party or a French party, a most serious and dangerous situation.
The Bill, moreover, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier said the other day, consists in nothing but a greater scope given to legislation already existing in our statute-books in a less extended form: and this legislation, according to his statement, is by no means extraordinary.
It is the inevitable sequel of our marvellous industrial, agricultural, commercial and political development.
The effect of the establisnment of this national navy will be to secure peace and harmony between the races; it will clearly demonstrate the loyalty of the Canadian people towards the motherland, who has granted to us and more especially to the people of the province of Quebec, national and religious privileges which neither independence, nor German allegiance, nor yet annexation to the United States could ever secure.
The measure entails no forced service on the part of the people of this country, nor the imposition of any new taxation, our ordinary public revenues being sufficient to meet the expenditure under this head.
All this _ is infinitely more1 akin to the Canadian ideal than would be the contribution of $25,000,000 proposed by the Conservative leader, inasmuch as it safeguards our autonomy and opposes the principle of imperial federation which appears at the root of that proposal.
Instead, therefore, of joining the standard of Mr. Borden, who proposes first of all a contribution of $25,000,000 and then the building of a navy at our own expense, but the control _ of which would remain with Great Britain, the people of Canada . will prefer to continue in their support of the eminent statesman who has been guiding our policy since fourteen years, securing at all times the greatness and prosperity of our country and who, in the present instance, is following in the footsteps of La-fontaine and Cartier.	*

DOHERTY (Montreal, St. Anne); Mr. Speaker before entering upon anything in the nature of an answer to the very able and eloquent address to which we have just listened with very great pleasure, whether we may have agreed or disagreed with the conclusions reached, I crave your permission to make a very brief reference to an incident that occurred this afternoon, and to some observations of my hon. friend the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I need not say that I have no concern with anything that the hon. member from Frontenac has thought proper to say reflecting upon the confidence which should or should not be reposed either in

the right hon. the leader of this House or any gentleman either on the other side or this side of the House, but I did listen, I have to say, with a great deal of pain, to some observations which that hon. gentleman found it proper to make. It was with very particular pleasure that I noted that at the conclusion of these observations the hon. gentleman very emphatically repudiated any desire whatever to reflect upon the loyalty of the French Canadian population of the province of Quebec.
Rats !

Some of the citations, however, which he thought proper to make, it seems to me should not be allowed to pass unanswered. I give him credit for not intending to reflect upon the loyalty of the population of Quebec.

You are too good.
Mr. DOHERTY-but I think that enough was said to make it quite proper that something should be said to do away with any false impression on that subject that might be created by the citations which the hon. gentleman thought proper to make. I take upon myself the duty of doing that with the greater pleasure because of the fact that I am not a French Canadian, and therefore am not directly concerned, and of the further fact, which is a fact, that from other points of view I may regret that I have not been able to reach precisely the same conclusions on the question which is formally before the House as have been reached by either mv French Canadian friends who sit on the other side of the House or by the French Canadians, or some of them, who sit on this side of the House. Thus in what I am about to say I am not speaking on either one side of this question or on the other. I have said I am not a French Canadian. I have, however, had the honour and the advantage to be born in a province largely French Canadian.

A'. WILSON. I do not know whether I quite understand the hon. member's remarks, but does he not think it in the public interest that the words that fell from the lips of the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) this afternoon, should be reproduced all over the country and in the ' Hansard,' at first?

I am not in a position to take upon myself to answer a question of that kind. I do not think it is for me to decide to what extent those words ought to be reproduced. For my own part, I think it is vastly more important that any false impression that might have been based on them should be wiped away at once, and that then both the words and the false -impression should be forgotten. However, it is for the hon. member for Laval
(Mr. C. A. Wilson) to exercise his own judgment as to whether he thinks that good will between the different races in this country would be furthered by the reproduction of words that seem to have given offence notwithstanding the fact of the declaration of the hon. member for Fron-tenac that he intended none.
However, I do not wish to be led into a discussion upon that question^ My desire is to say this much in correction of any false impression that might be derived from the citations made by the hon. memlber. I was about to say that although I am' not a French Canadian, I have the honour and advantage of having been borne in a province largely populated by French Canadians. I have' had the pleasure and the advantage of living with and among French Canadians all my life. I think I can claim to know the French Canadian population of the province of Quebec as well as any man who is not of their race, and I am here to say that everything that I have known of them has been of a nature to create the most absolute confidence in their most unrestricted loyalty to their country and to the Crown under which we all live. I have had the advantage not only of knowing them and living among them in civil life, but I have had the pleasure and the honour of serving with them in the rebellion of 1885 in a purely French Canadian regiment, the 65th Battalion, and I can certify that no braver, no more competent, no more devoted soldiers went out to maintain the cause of this country in that rebellion, than my French Canadian fellow countrymen.
The matter to which I wish especially to refer is a work and what purported to be a citation from that work. I had the pleasure and advantage of knowing Reverend Father Hamon whose work purported to be cited here this afternoon, I would point out in the first place that Father Hamon was not a French Canadian. I do not want to say that to his discredit, because he was a friend of mine, a gentleman for whom I entertained the highest respect; but Father Hamon was a Frenchman, and as a Frenchman would have been at liberty, without its reflecting in any way on the loyalty of the French Canadians, to express what aspirations he might choose with regard to the future of the -French speaking race on the continent of America. But we need not stop at that, because I have been at pains to send for the work, I have turned to the chapter cited, chapter 18, and I have carefully gone through that and there is not one word _ in that chapter that is susceptible of being contorted into what was cited as having been written by Father Hamon. With the other work referred to I am not familiaT.

With the permission of the hon. gentleman I want to say that I quoted what purported to be a correct English translation of that work. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty) says that that was not a correct translation of that work, I gladly accept his assurance to that effect. I do not want to misrepresent any one.

I wish to say not only is it not a correct translation, but that there is nothing, absolutely nothing, in the language to warrant the interpretation given to it. I do not pretend to have read all the book, but I have read the chapter from which this purports to be taken, and I have found that it has been distorted m such a manner in the translation as to give a false idea of what it contains but of course we cannot hold my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) responsible, and he no doubt gave his citations in perfect good faith. So far from there being any suggestion in these chapters of the formation of a French republic, the writer showed _ the most careful reserve against expressing any opinion regarding the future from a political point of view of the French Canadian race, either in the New England States-and it was of _ these the reverend gentleman was writing-or in the province of Quebec. With regard to the other work mentioned,
I have not read it, but I certainly have never seen any reflection or re-echo of its effects among the French Canadians of the province of Quebec, such as one might expect, if the work were as extreme as is suggested; but if my hon. friend is relying on a translation, my experience of a per-usual of the other book which he quoted may possibly set him right with regard to the last one. I do not wish to push that matter further. We have had some reference to another question-the speech of a late leading political man in the province of Quebec. But, however, people may view the politics or life work of that man, it was after that work had been completed and after he had [DOT] been, rightly or wrongly, sweet from power by the almost unanimous vote of his fellow countrymen that he gave expression to the views my hon. friend from Frontenac has just cited, so that I do not think any possible inference can be drawn from the ^expression of those views whereby they might be supposed to represent the sentiments of the French Canadian population. I must apologize for having gone into this matter, which of course is not pertinent to the subject before us for discussion, but I felt it was incumbent upon me to do what little lay in my power to prevent any misconception which might give rise to any feeling of prejudice as between the different races occupying this country.

Haying disposed of this little matter and knowing it would be quite impossible for me to do justice to the important subject before the House, on which we are called to express as fully as we can our views, I would respectfully beg, Mr. Speaker, to move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to.
